questions.stem: The ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle believed that mental processes such as thought and emotion were located in the:
options: pineal gland
heart
brain
liver
questions.explanation: Aristotle held the heart hypothesis, believing the brain's main job was to cool the blood. Others, such as Hippocrates, argued for the brain hypothesis, which later research supported.

questions.stem: Descartes proposed that the mind and body are separate but interact. Where did he suggest this interaction takes place?
options: the pineal gland
the cerebellum
the heart
the corpus callosum
questions.explanation: Descartes' dualism held that the non-physical mind and the physical body interact through the pineal gland. The heart was the seat of the mind in Aristotle's much earlier view, not in Descartes' theory.

questions.stem: Phrenology, developed by Franz Gall, claimed that:
options: brain areas could be mapped by electrically stimulating the cortex
speech production depends mainly on an area located in the left frontal lobe
the mind and body are separate and interact in the pineal gland
bumps on the skull revealed a person's mental abilities and character
questions.explanation: Phrenologists measured the bumps and shape of the skull, believing each reflected the size of a brain area responsible for a trait. Electrical stimulation of the cortex was used much later, notably by Penfield, and gave far more valid evidence about brain function.

questions.stem: Phrenology is now rejected as a way of understanding the brain. The main reason is that:
options: it claimed that every area of the brain performs exactly the same function as the others
it relied on brain scans that were too blurry to show the bumps on the skull clearly
it located all mental processes in the heart rather than anywhere in the brain at all
the shape of the skull does not reflect the size or function of the brain areas beneath it
questions.explanation: Research showed that skull shape tells us nothing about the underlying brain or a person's abilities. Phrenology did assume that different areas have different functions, an idea of localisation that was partly right, so it is not rejected for treating all areas as the same.

questions.stem: In 1861, Broca examined the brain of a patient who could understand speech but could say little more than the syllable 'tan'. Broca found damage in the:
options: left occipital lobe
left frontal lobe
left temporal lobe
right frontal lobe
questions.explanation: The patient's damage was in an area of the left frontal lobe now called Broca's area, which is involved in producing speech. Damage to the left temporal lobe, in Wernicke's area, affects understanding speech rather than producing it.

questions.stem: After a stroke, Glen speaks fluently, but his sentences make little sense and he has trouble understanding what others say. Which area is most likely damaged?
options: the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe
the cerebellum in the hindbrain
Wernicke's area in the left temporal lobe
Broca's area in the left frontal lobe
questions.explanation: Wernicke's area is involved in comprehending language, so damage there produces fluent but meaningless speech and poor understanding. Damage to Broca's area produces slow, effortful speech while comprehension is largely kept, which is the opposite of Glen's pattern.

questions.stem: During surgery for epilepsy, Penfield electrically stimulated the cortex of conscious patients and recorded what they reported or did. This allowed him to:
options: map the functions of areas such as the motor and somatosensory cortex
measure the blood flow in active brain areas while patients did tasks
show that the skull's shape reflects the size of brain areas below
prove that the mind and body are separate and do not interact
questions.explanation: Stimulating a point in the motor cortex made a body part move and stimulating the somatosensory cortex produced sensations, so Penfield could map these areas. Measuring blood flow during tasks is what fMRI does, a technique that came decades later.

questions.stem: In 1848, an iron rod passed through Phineas Gage's left frontal lobe. He survived, but friends said he became impulsive, rude and unreliable. This case provided early evidence that the frontal lobe is involved in:
options: the control of heart rate and breathing
personality and the regulation of behaviour
the coordination of balance and posture
the processing of sound and speech
questions.explanation: Gage's change in personality after frontal lobe damage suggested that this area helps regulate behaviour and emotion. Balance and posture depend mainly on the cerebellum, and heart rate and breathing on the brainstem, both of which were not damaged.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to find out which brain areas become more active while participants solve puzzles. Why would she choose fMRI rather than CT?
options: CT shows brain structure only, while fMRI shows changes in activity
CT uses strong magnets that would distract participants doing puzzles
fMRI uses X-rays, which give a much sharper image of the brain
CT can image the brainstem but not the cerebral cortex
questions.explanation: CT produces static images of brain structure using X-rays, so it cannot show which areas are working during a task, whereas fMRI tracks activity over time. The distractors mix up the technologies: CT uses X-rays and MRI uses magnets.

questions.stem: In a split-brain patient, a word is flashed only to the left visual field. The patient says they saw nothing but can pick out the named object with their left hand. Why?
options: The cut corpus callosum stops all visual information from reaching the cortex
The right hemisphere controls speech, but it cannot recognise written words
The word reached the right hemisphere, but speech is mainly controlled by the left
The word reached the left hemisphere, but the left hand is controlled by the right
questions.explanation: Information from the left visual field goes to the right hemisphere, which controls the left hand, so the patient can select the object by touch. With the corpus callosum cut, the information cannot cross to the left hemisphere, where speech is mainly produced, so the patient cannot name it.

questions.stem: Which hindbrain structure controls vital automatic functions such as heart rate, blood pressure and swallowing?
options: cerebellum
thalamus
medulla
pons
questions.explanation: The medulla, at the base of the brainstem, controls vital survival functions, which is why damage to it can be fatal. The cerebellum is also in the hindbrain, but it coordinates movement and balance rather than these vital functions.

questions.stem: The pons is a hindbrain structure that:
options: coordinates fine movements and maintains balance and posture
receives sensory information from the senses and relays it on to the cerebral cortex
regulates hunger, thirst and body temperature for homeostasis
relays messages between the cerebrum and cerebellum and helps regulate sleep
questions.explanation: The pons acts as a bridge between the cerebrum and the cerebellum and is involved in sleep, dreaming and breathing. Coordinating fine movement and balance is the role of the cerebellum, which sits behind the pons.

questions.stem: After a stroke, Ruth can still move her limbs, but she loses her balance easily, her movements are jerky and she cannot touch her nose accurately. Which structure is most likely damaged?
options: cerebellum
medulla
primary motor cortex
thalamus
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates the timing and accuracy of movements and maintains balance, so damage produces clumsy, uncoordinated movement. Damage to the primary motor cortex would cause weakness or paralysis, but Ruth can still move her limbs.

questions.stem: The reticular formation, a network of neurons running through the midbrain and hindbrain, is mainly involved in:
options: coordinating fine motor skills and maintaining balance
producing fluent speech and understanding language
regulating hunger, thirst and body temperature
arousal, alertness and filtering incoming sensory information
questions.explanation: The reticular formation keeps us awake and alert and helps filter out unimportant sensory information. Hunger, thirst and temperature are regulated by the hypothalamus in the forebrain.

questions.stem: Parkinson's disease involves the loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra. The substantia nigra is part of the:
options: cerebellum
midbrain
hindbrain
cerebral cortex
questions.explanation: The substantia nigra is a midbrain structure whose dopamine-producing neurons help control smooth, voluntary movement. Parkinson's disease is a movement disorder, but its key loss is not in the cerebellum, which coordinates movement in a different way.

questions.stem: Which forebrain structure acts as a relay station, receiving information from all the senses except smell and sending it to the cerebral cortex?
options: pons
thalamus
hypothalamus
amygdala
questions.explanation: The thalamus relays sensory information to the relevant areas of the cortex; smell is the one sense that largely bypasses it. The hypothalamus sits just below it and regulates homeostasis rather than relaying sensory information.

questions.stem: A tumour disrupts Ben's regulation of body temperature, hunger and thirst. Which forebrain structure is most likely affected?
options: amygdala
cerebral cortex
hypothalamus
thalamus
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus maintains homeostasis by regulating body temperature, hunger, thirst and the release of hormones through the pituitary gland. The thalamus, despite its similar name, relays sensory information and does not regulate these drives.

questions.stem: In which lobe of the cerebral cortex is the primary motor cortex located?
options: parietal lobe
temporal lobe
occipital lobe
frontal lobe
questions.explanation: The primary motor cortex is a strip at the back of the frontal lobe that initiates voluntary movements. The strip just behind it, in the parietal lobe, is the primary somatosensory cortex, which receives touch sensations.

questions.stem: A stroke damages the primary motor cortex in Ali's left hemisphere. Which outcome is most likely?
options: loss of hearing in his left ear only
weakness or paralysis on the right side of his body
weakness or paralysis on the left side of his body
loss of touch sensation on the left side of his body
questions.explanation: Each hemisphere's motor cortex controls voluntary movement on the opposite side of the body, so left hemisphere damage affects the right side. Loss of touch sensation would follow damage to the somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe, not the motor cortex.

questions.stem: On the primary somatosensory cortex, the lips and fingertips are represented by much larger areas than the back. Why?
options: Their signals reach the brain without passing through the thalamus
They have more sensory receptors and so are more sensitive
They cover a larger area of skin than the back does
Their nerves do not cross over to the opposite hemisphere
questions.explanation: The size of an area on the somatosensory cortex reflects the sensitivity of the body part, which depends on its number of receptors, not its physical size. The back is much larger than the lips but is far less sensitive, so it has a small area.

questions.stem: A tennis player decides to return a serve and swings smoothly and accurately. Which statement correctly matches brain areas with their roles?
options: The thalamus initiates the swing; the pons coordinates its timing
The primary motor cortex initiates the swing; the cerebellum coordinates it
The cerebellum initiates the swing; the primary motor cortex coordinates it
The occipital lobe initiates the swing; the medulla coordinates it
questions.explanation: Voluntary movements are initiated by the primary motor cortex in the frontal lobe, while the cerebellum fine-tunes their timing, balance and accuracy. Reversing these roles is a common error; the cerebellum adjusts movements but does not start them.

questions.stem: Kira reads a sentence aloud. Which sequence best describes the path of information in her cortex?
options: motor cortex, then Broca's area, then Wernicke's area, then visual cortex
Wernicke's area, then visual cortex, then motor cortex, then Broca's area
visual cortex, then Wernicke's area, then Broca's area, then motor cortex
Broca's area, then Wernicke's area, then visual cortex, then motor cortex
questions.explanation: The words are first processed in the occipital lobe's visual cortex, then understood in Wernicke's area, then a plan for speech is formed in Broca's area, which signals the motor cortex to move the speech muscles. Comprehension must come before speech is planned, so Broca's area cannot come first.

questions.stem: Which part of the cerebral cortex is most involved in planning, decision-making and regulating emotional responses?
options: primary auditory cortex
somatosensory cortex
prefrontal cortex
primary visual cortex
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex, at the front of the frontal lobe, handles higher-order functions such as planning, judgement and controlling emotional reactions. The other areas mainly receive and process sensory information.

questions.stem: When a person sees a threatening face, the amygdala responds quickly, and the prefrontal cortex can then moderate the response. Because the prefrontal cortex is one of the last areas to mature, adolescents are more likely than adults to:
options: lose the function of the amygdala during the teenage years
respond emotionally and impulsively in some situations
show no emotional response at all to threatening faces
rely on the cerebellum when making complex decisions
questions.explanation: While the prefrontal cortex is still maturing, the amygdala has relatively more influence, so adolescents can react more emotionally and impulsively. The amygdala keeps working throughout adolescence; it is the regulating role of the prefrontal cortex that is still developing.

questions.stem: Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to:
options: grow new lobes when an area of the cortex has been damaged
protect itself from injury using the skull and fluid around it
change its structure and function in response to experience or injury
keep exactly the same neural connections throughout life once they have formed
questions.explanation: Neuroplasticity means the brain can reorganise its neural connections throughout life as a result of learning, experience and damage. The brain does not grow new lobes; plasticity works at the level of connections between neurons.

questions.stem: During brain development, synaptic pruning refers to the:
options: coating of axons with a fatty, insulating layer
movement of new neurons to their final positions
elimination of weak or unused synaptic connections
growth of new dendrites and axon branches to form extra connections
questions.explanation: In synaptic pruning, connections that are rarely used are removed, making the remaining networks more efficient. Coating axons with fatty insulation is myelination, a different process that speeds up transmission.

questions.stem: During adolescence, myelination continues in areas such as the prefrontal cortex. What is the main effect of this?
options: Unused connections between neurons are removed
New neurons are produced to replace old ones
The cortex becomes thinner and less active
Neural messages travel faster and more efficiently
questions.explanation: Myelin insulates axons so that neural impulses travel faster and more efficiently. Removing unused connections is synaptic pruning, which also happens in adolescence but is a separate process.

questions.stem: Which area of the brain is generally the last to fully mature?
options: primary visual cortex
medulla
thalamus
prefrontal cortex
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex continues to mature into the mid-twenties, which is linked to adolescents' developing judgement and impulse control. Structures such as the medulla, which control vital functions, are mature very early.

questions.stem: After a stroke, an undamaged neuron that has lost its connection with a damaged neuron forms a new connection with another active neuron. This process is called:
options: synaptic pruning
myelination
rerouting
sprouting
questions.explanation: Rerouting is when an undamaged neuron connects with a different active neuron after losing its link to a damaged one. Sprouting is the growth of new branches on axons or dendrites, which creates extra connections rather than redirecting an existing one.

questions.stem: After brain injury, neurons near the damaged area grow new branches on their axons and dendrites, allowing new connections to form. This is called:
options: synaptic pruning
neural migration
sprouting
rerouting
questions.explanation: Sprouting is the growth of new extensions on a neuron that allow it to make new connections, helping to compensate for damage. Rerouting involves an undamaged neuron forming a new connection after losing a link, rather than growing new branches.

questions.stem: A four-year-old and a sixty-year-old suffer similar damage to the language areas of the left hemisphere. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Neither regains any language, because plasticity ends soon after birth
The child regains more language, because the young brain is more plastic
The adult regains more language, because adults have far more neurons
Both regain the same amount, because plasticity is constant across life
questions.explanation: Neuroplasticity is greatest early in life, so a young child's brain is better able to reorganise and shift functions such as language to other areas. Plasticity continues in adults, but to a lesser degree, so the claim that it ends after birth is false.

questions.stem: London taxi drivers who spent years learning the city's routes were found to have a larger posterior hippocampus than people who did not drive taxis. This is best described as evidence of:
options: adaptive plasticity resulting from experience
developmental plasticity during early infancy
synaptic pruning of rarely used pathways
an acquired brain injury caused by stress
questions.explanation: Adaptive plasticity is the brain's ability to change in response to learning and experience, here the demands of memorising routes. Developmental plasticity refers to changes that occur as part of normal development, especially in early life, not to adult learning.

questions.stem: Rats raised in large cages with toys, ladders and other rats developed a thicker cortex than rats raised alone in bare cages. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Living alone damages the cortex by causing an acquired brain injury
The number of neurons in the cortex is fixed at birth in all mammals
An enriched environment can increase the growth of neural connections
A thick cortex is inherited and determines which rats seek out toys
questions.explanation: The rats were assigned to their environments, so the difference in the cortex can be attributed to the enriched environment, which stimulated the growth of connections. The inheritance explanation does not fit, because the researchers, not the rats, decided which environment each rat lived in.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to help maintain brain functioning as a person ages?
options: avoiding challenging tasks so that neurons are not overworked
repeating only familiar tasks to strengthen existing pathways
staying awake for longer each night to give the brain extra practice time
regular aerobic exercise, which increases blood flow to the brain
questions.explanation: Physical exercise improves blood flow to the brain and is linked to better brain health, alongside mental stimulation, social connection and sleep. Avoiding challenges works against plasticity, because new learning is what builds and maintains neural connections.

questions.stem: An acquired brain injury (ABI) is best defined as:
options: a brain difference inherited through the genes
a change in the brain caused only by ageing
damage to the brain that occurs after birth
damage to the brain that is present at birth
questions.explanation: An ABI is any damage to the brain that happens after birth, from causes such as accidents, stroke, lack of oxygen or infection. Damage present at birth is not acquired, so it falls outside this definition.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-traumatic acquired brain injury?
options: a fall from a ladder
a car accident
a blow to the head in football
a stroke
questions.explanation: Non-traumatic ABIs come from causes inside the body, such as a stroke, tumour, infection or lack of oxygen. Falls, car accidents and blows to the head apply external force, so they cause traumatic brain injuries.

questions.stem: Two years after a traumatic brain injury, Nikhil has lost his job and several friendships because of his irritability. In terms of the biopsychosocial approach, the loss of his job and friendships is a:
options: biological impact
psychological impact
hereditary impact
social impact
questions.explanation: Effects on a person's relationships, work and place in the community are social impacts of an ABI. His irritability itself is a psychological impact; the loss of friends and work is the social consequence that follows.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a biological impact of an acquired brain injury?
options: difficulty concentrating on a task
withdrawal from friends and sport
seizures and reduced control of one arm
low mood and feelings of frustration
questions.explanation: Biological impacts are physical effects on the body and nervous system, such as seizures, fatigue and motor problems. Difficulty concentrating is a cognitive effect, so it is a psychological impact even though it results from physical damage.

questions.stem: Which set of symptoms is most typical of Parkinson's disease?
options: tremor, muscle rigidity and slowness of movement
memory loss, confusion and difficulty finding words
sudden seizures with loss of consciousness
muscle weakness and blurred vision that come and go
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease is a movement disorder caused by the loss of dopamine-producing neurons, producing tremor, rigidity and slowed movement. Memory loss and confusion are the main early features of dementias such as Alzheimer's disease.

questions.stem: L-dopa is used to treat the symptoms of Parkinson's disease because it:
options: blocks dopamine from acting on neurons
is converted into dopamine in the brain
replaces the serotonin lost from the cerebellum
regrows dead neurons in the substantia nigra
questions.explanation: Dopamine itself cannot cross from the blood into the brain, but L-dopa can, and it is then converted into dopamine, easing movement symptoms. It does not regrow the lost neurons, which is why the disease continues to progress.

questions.stem: Research suggests that the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease often appear only years after the disease process begins. The best explanation is that:
options: the brain produces extra dopamine neurons in the early stages
many dopamine neurons are lost before movement is noticeably affected
the disease begins in the cerebellum and spreads to the midbrain later
dopamine neurons are lost only after the first symptoms appear
questions.explanation: The remaining dopamine neurons can compensate for a time, so symptoms appear only after a large proportion have been lost. This is why researchers are looking for early signs of the disease, so that treatment might begin sooner.

questions.stem: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is associated with:
options: a lack of oxygen to the brain during birth or in early infancy
repeated head impacts, including ones that do not cause concussion
a single severe concussion that resolves fully within a few weeks
an inherited gene mutation that is present from the time of birth
questions.explanation: CTE is linked to repeated blows to the head, such as those in contact sports, including subconcussive impacts that produce no obvious symptoms. It is progressive rather than something that resolves, and it is acquired through head impacts rather than inherited.

questions.stem: When CTE is diagnosed by examining brain tissue after death, what do researchers look for?
options: amyloid plaques spread evenly through the whole cortex
loss of dopamine neurons limited to the substantia nigra
a single large bleed in one side of the cerebrum
an abnormal build-up of tau protein around blood vessels
questions.explanation: CTE is identified by a characteristic pattern of abnormal tau protein, often clustered around small blood vessels in the cortex. Amyloid plaques are a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, and dopamine neuron loss is the key feature of Parkinson's disease.

questions.stem: Which statement about CTE is correct?
options: It is progressive, and symptoms can appear years after the head impacts stopped
It is caused by one severe concussion, and symptoms clear within a few weeks
It is caused by a gene mutation and its symptoms are present from early childhood
It mainly damages the spinal cord, so its symptoms are physical rather than mental
questions.explanation: CTE worsens over time, and changes in memory, mood and behaviour may appear many years after a person's playing career ends. It affects the brain and produces cognitive and emotional symptoms such as memory loss, depression and impulsivity, not mainly physical ones.

questions.stem: Many studies of CTE use brains donated to brain banks by the families of former contact-sport players. Why must the rates of CTE found in these studies be interpreted with caution?
options: CTE is found only in professional boxers, so other sports cannot be studied in this way
The samples include too many people who never experienced any head impacts in their lives
Families who were worried about symptoms are more likely to donate, so the sample is biased
Brain tissue examined after death cannot show the tau protein that is used to identify CTE
questions.explanation: Donated brains often come from players who showed symptoms during life, so the sample is not representative and the rate of CTE may be overestimated. Post-mortem examination is in fact the way CTE is confirmed, because that is when tau deposits can be seen directly.
